summary: A doubly landlocked country in the heart of Central Asia, where the ancient Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva preserve a wealth of Islamic architecture; it was once the center of the Timurid Empire and became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: In the early 8th century Arab armies conquered Transoxiana, and Samarkand and Bukhara gradually became centers of learning in the Islamic world; in the 9th century al-Bukhari of Bukhara compiled the most important collection of Sunni hadith, and in the 14th century Baha ad-Din Naqshband of Bukhara founded the far-reaching Sufi order. During the Soviet period mosques were closed, and in 1927 the "Hujum" campaign of forced unveiling was carried out. After independence in 1991 Islam revived, but the Karimov government long kept independent religious activity under tight control, and restrictions have been relaxed only gradually in recent years.

ranking.name: Others (including no religion)
ranking.description: Seventy years of Soviet atheist education left many people belonging to a religion only nominally, or not believing at all. There are also other minority faiths: among the Koreans forcibly moved from the Far East to Central Asia by Stalin in 1937 were many Protestants, while the ancient Bukharan Jewish community largely emigrated to Israel and the United States in the 1990s, shrinking greatly in number.

ranking.name: Russian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In 1865 the Russian Empire captured Tashkent and then conquered Central Asia, and Russian officials, soldiers and settlers brought Orthodoxy. In the Soviet period, population evacuated during the Second World War and workers who came to rebuild after the 1966 Tashkent earthquake further increased the Russian population. After independence in 1991 many Russians emigrated, so the Orthodox share fell, and it is concentrated mainly in large cities such as Tashkent.

religion.background: The ancient Uzbek lands belonged to Sogdian and Khwarazmian culture, where Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and Manichaeism were popular. After the Arab conquest in the 8th century Islam became the mainstream, Samarkand and Bukhara became major centers of Islamic learning and Sufism, and in the 14th century the Timurid Empire built magnificent mosques and madrasas in Samarkand. Russian conquest in the 19th century brought Orthodoxy, and the Soviet period promoted atheism. After independence Islam has been regarded as part of national cultural tradition, but the government still maintains tight control over religious activity.

ranking.name: Uzbek
ranking.description: Uzbek belongs to the Karluk branch of the Turkic family and derives from Chagatai, the medieval Central Asian language; in the 15th century the poet Navoi wrote in Chagatai and is revered as the father of Uzbek literature. In 1924 the Soviet Union established the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, and the script changed from Arabic to Latin (1928), then to Cyrillic (1940), and after independence in 1993 it was decided to change back to Latin. Uzbeks make up over 80 percent of the country, so it is the mother tongue of the majority.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Under tsarist Russia and the Soviet Union, Russian was the language of administration, science and higher education, and elites in cities such as Tashkent were generally educated in Russian. After independence in 1991 Uzbek became the sole state language and many Russians emigrated, so the number of native Russian speakers fell; but Russian is still widely used in business, the media and urban life, and is essential for those who go to work in Russia.

ranking.name: Tajik
ranking.description: Samarkand and Bukhara have been Persian-speaking cities since ancient times; when the Soviet Union drew the borders of the Central Asian national states in 1924, they were assigned to Uzbekistan, and under assimilation policies in the Soviet period and after independence many local Tajiks registered as Uzbeks. The actual number of Tajik speakers is therefore probably higher than the statistics show, concentrated mainly in these two historic cities and surrounding areas.

ranking.name: Kazakh
ranking.description: Kazakhs live mainly in the Karakalpakstan autonomous republic in the west and in regions bordering Kazakhstan such as Tashkent Region, and traditionally lived as nomads. When the Soviet Union drew the borders, these Kazakh-populated areas were assigned to Uzbekistan, forming today's minority community; after independence some also moved back to Kazakhstan.

language.history: In ancient Uzbek lands, East Iranian languages such as Sogdian and Khwarazmian were spoken, and as Turkic tribes moved south and the region became Islamized, Turkic and Persian gradually became dominant. Chagatai, formed in the Middle Ages, was the common written language of the Central Asian Turkic peoples, and the works of Navoi in the 15th century were its peak. In the Soviet period modern Uzbek was standardized on the basis of the Tashkent dialect, and the script changed first to Latin and then to Cyrillic. In 1989 Uzbek became the state language, and from 1993 a return to the Latin alphabet has been promoted, though the two scripts still coexist today.

ranking.name: Uzbek plov
ranking.description: Lamb, onions and yellow carrot strips are stir-fried in oil in a large cauldron, then rice, chickpeas, raisins and whole garlic are added and steamed until done, giving glossy, richly fragrant rice.
ranking.history: Plov is a dish shared along the Silk Road, and folk legend links it with Alexander the Great or with the physician Ibn Sina, who came from the Bukhara area. In Uzbekistan, on the morning of a wedding a huge pot of "morning plov" is first prepared for male guests, enjoyed by hundreds together; there is also a custom of making plov at home every Thursday. In 2016 "Culture and traditions of Oshi Palov" was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and Tashkent even has a Plov Center specializing in cooking plov in large quantities.

ranking.name: Samsa
ranking.description: Layered dough is filled with diced lamb, mutton fat and onion, pinched into triangles and baked against the wall of a tandoor (clay oven), with a crisp crust and juicy filling.
ranking.history: This filled pastry is called "sanbosa" in Persian and spread with Silk Road traders throughout Central Asia, the Middle East and South Asia, becoming the deep-fried triangular samosa in India. The Uzbek version continues the Central Asian tradition of baking in a tandoor, and depending on the season there are also fillings of pumpkin or green wild herbs. Today samsa is the most common snack at markets, street stalls and teahouses, often eaten with green tea.

ranking.name: Lagman
ranking.description: Hand-pulled thick noodles are boiled and topped with a thick sauce stir-fried from lamb or beef, bell pepper, tomato, radish and garlic; the noodles are chewy.
ranking.history: Lagman derives from the hand-pulled noodles of the Uyghurs of Xinjiang and the Hui (Dungans), and its name has the same origin as the Chinese "lamian." After the failure of the Hui uprisings in Qing-dynasty northwest China in the late 19th century, large numbers of Dungans and Uyghurs moved into Russian Central Asia, bringing the technique of pulled noodles to places such as the Fergana Valley. In Uzbekistan it has gradually merged into local cuisine and is a noodle dish common in restaurants and homes today.

ranking.name: Manti
ranking.description: Thin dough wrappers are filled with chopped lamb, mutton fat and onion, sometimes with pumpkin, steamed in a multi-tiered steamer and eaten with yogurt or vinegar.
ranking.history: The name manti is related to words such as the Chinese "mantou"; it is generally believed to have come to Central Asia with the Silk Road and the exchanges of the Mongol Empire period, and later became widespread among Turkic-speaking peoples. The Central Asian version is filled with lamb and mutton fat and bursts with juice when bitten. During the Soviet period multi-tiered aluminum steamers became common in households, and manti became a regular dish at festivals and family gatherings.

ranking.name: Shashlik (kebab)
ranking.description: Lamb, beef or lamb liver is cut into pieces, marinated, skewered on iron sticks and grilled over charcoal until browned outside and tender inside, eaten with raw onion, vinegar and non (bread).
ranking.history: Central Asian nomadic and oasis peoples have a long history of grilling meat on skewers, and the name "shashlik" spread through Russian, becoming the name used throughout the Soviet Union in the Soviet period. In Uzbek "chaikhanas" (teahouses), kebabs, green tea and non are the classic combination for men's social gatherings. Grill stalls at markets and along highways are also found everywhere, making it one of the most common meals eaten out.
